title: Two Together: How Pairing Switches an RTK On

scenes.visual: Dark slate frame filled 70% vertically by a cross-section of a grey plasma membrane bilayer with a single teal receptor tyrosine kinase spanning it, its amber cytoplasmic kinase glowing dimly. Bold white title 'Two Together: How Pairing Switches an RTK On' sits cleanly above the membrane, fading out at 2 seconds. Small 'Schematic' tag in corner.

scenes.tts: A growth factor floats outside the cell and never crosses the membrane. Only one narrow helix connects outside to inside. So how does a signal outside switch on an enzyme on the far side? For receptor tyrosine kinases, the answer begins by bringing two receptors together.
scenes.caption: A growth factor floats outside the cell and never crosses the membrane. Only one narrow helix connects outside to inside. So how does a signal outside switch on an enzyme on the far side? For receptor tyrosine kinases, the answer begins by bringing two receptors together.
scenes.visual: Same membrane cross-section. A sky-blue growth factor drifts gently in the upper extracellular space without crossing the grey bilayer. A pulse highlights the single narrow teal transmembrane helix, then the camera pans slightly as a second identical teal receptor drifts into view from the right.
scenes.narration: A growth factor floats outside the cell and never crosses the membrane. Only one narrow helix connects outside to inside. So how does a signal outside switch on an enzyme on the far side? For receptor tyrosine kinases, the answer begins by bringing two receptors together.

scenes.tts: Every receptor tyrosine kinase shares one three-part plan. Outside sits the ectodomain that catches the ligand. One helix spans the membrane. Inside hangs a kinase with a small upper lobe and a large lower lobe, plus a tail carrying tyrosines. Left alone, that kinase holds itself shut. In the insulin receptor, a flexible stretch called the activation loop plugs its own active site.

scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly onto one teal receptor filling 65% of frame height. High-contrast labels (size 28+, max 4 words) appear as each part lights up: 'Ectodomain' (teal top), 'Single helix' (teal span), 'Two-lobed kinase' (amber bottom) with 'Tail (tyrosines)' drifting softly below. Inside the amber cleft, a coral-red strand labelled 'Activation loop (insulin receptor)' folds tightly across the active site. Empathy fix: Label the amber kinase's two lobes 'Small lobe' (upper) and 'Large lobe' (lower) as they are named, and keep both labels visible through s06; the coral plug is labelled 'Activation loop'.
scenes.narration: Every receptor tyrosine kinase shares one three-part plan. Outside sits the ectodomain that catches the ligand. One helix spans the membrane. Inside hangs a kinase with a small upper lobe and a large lower lobe, plus a tail carrying tyrosines. Left alone, that kinase holds itself shut. In the insulin receptor, a flexible stretch called the activation loop plugs its own active site.

scenes.tts: To release that brake, cells bring two kinases together in at least three ways. Some ligands, like nerve growth factor, are built as pairs that bridge two receptors. Epidermal growth factor binds one receptor and opens a hidden arm, so two receptor arms clasp together.
scenes.caption: To release that brake, cells bring two kinases together in at least three ways. Some ligands, like nerve growth factor, are built as pairs that bridge two receptors. Epidermal growth factor binds one receptor and opens a hidden arm, so two receptor arms clasp together.
scenes.visual: Keep the same membrane cross-section and animate the first two routes in sequence (labelled 'Schematic'). First, a sky-blue two-part ligand ('NGF dimer') bridges two teal ectodomains, pulling their amber kinases together. Then morph smoothly: two folded teal ectodomains each catch one sky-blue EGF dot on their outer faces, swing open their tucked teal 'Dimerization arms', and clasp arm-to-arm while the two EGF dots stay apart.
scenes.narration: To release that brake, cells bring two kinases together in at least three ways. Some ligands, like nerve growth factor, are built as pairs that bridge two receptors. Epidermal growth factor binds one receptor and opens a hidden arm, so two receptor arms clasp together.

scenes.tts: The insulin receptor works differently. Its two halves are already joined by disulfide bonds, with their kinase legs held apart at rest. Binding insulin shifts the whole shape, pulling those inner legs together. All three routes end in the same place: two resting kinases side by side.
scenes.caption: The insulin receptor works differently. Its two halves are already joined by disulfide bonds, with their kinase legs held apart at rest. Binding insulin shifts the whole shape, pulling those inner legs together. All three routes end in the same place: two resting kinases side by side.
scenes.visual: Morph the teal pair into a pre-linked insulin receptor joined outside by short white disulfide bars, its two transmembrane legs splayed apart so the amber kinases cannot touch. Sky-blue insulin docks into the outer pocket; the legs pivot inward smoothly until the two amber kinases sit side by side beneath the membrane.
scenes.narration: The insulin receptor works differently. Its two halves are already joined by disulfide bonds, with their kinase legs held apart at rest. Binding insulin shifts the whole shape, pulling those inner legs together. All three routes end in the same place: two resting kinases side by side.

scenes.tts: Now the paired kinases release each other's brake. In the insulin receptor and most others, each kinase adds phosphates to the activation loop of its partner. Those phosphates swing the blocking loop clear of the cleft. The two lobes close on ATP, and catalysis begins.
scenes.caption: Now the paired kinases release each other's brake. In the insulin receptor and most others, each kinase adds phosphates to the activation loop of its partner. Those phosphates swing the blocking loop clear of the cleft. The two lobes close on ATP, and catalysis begins.
scenes.visual: Zoom in on the two side-by-side amber kinases with coral-red loops plugging their clefts. Bright yellow phosphate circles ('P') transfer across from each kinase to the partner's coral loop (labelled 'Trans-autophosphorylation'). Three yellow phosphates appear on each loop, the coral loops swing wide open, yellow ATP settles into each cleft, and both amber kinases brighten to active gold.
scenes.narration: Now the paired kinases release each other's brake. In the insulin receptor and most others, each kinase adds phosphates to the activation loop of its partner. Those phosphates swing the blocking loop clear of the cleft. The two lobes close on ATP, and catalysis begins.

scenes.tts: The epidermal growth factor receptor breaks that pattern. It needs no phosphate on its activation loop. Instead, the two kinases form a lopsided pair. The large lobe of one kinase presses against the small lobe of its neighbor. That push opens only the pressed copy into its active shape.
scenes.caption: The epidermal growth factor receptor breaks that pattern. It needs no phosphate on its activation loop. Instead, the two kinases form a lopsided pair. The large lobe of one kinase presses against the small lobe of its neighbor. That push opens only the pressed copy into its active shape.
scenes.visual: Transition smoothly to two amber EGF-receptor kinases with coral loops still unphosphorylated. The left kinase tilts so its bottom 'Large lobe' presses firmly against the top 'Small lobe' of the right kinase (labelled 'Asymmetric pair'). Only the pressed right kinase clicks open and glows bright gold, while the pressing left kinase stays dim amber.
scenes.narration: The epidermal growth factor receptor breaks that pattern. It needs no phosphate on its activation loop. Instead, the two kinases form a lopsided pair. The large lobe of one kinase presses against the small lobe of its neighbor. That push opens only the pressed copy into its active shape.

scenes.tts: Notice that division of labor. The pressing copy only needs to supply a surface. Now pause and predict. Her two and Her three are relatives of the epidermal growth factor receptor. Her two has a working kinase; Her three barely has one. If Her two pairs with Her three, can that mixed pair still switch on?
scenes.caption: Notice that division of labor. The pressing copy only needs to supply a surface. Now pause and predict. HER2 and HER3 are relatives of the epidermal growth factor receptor. HER2 has a working kinase; HER3 barely has one. If HER2 pairs with HER3, can that mixed pair still switch on?
scenes.visual: Replace the left teal/amber receptor with a violet receptor labelled 'HER3' whose catalytic cleft is softly hatched and labelled 'Nearly inactive', facing a teal/amber receptor labelled 'HER2'. A clean dark overlay banner at top displays the question: 'Can HER2 + HER3 still switch on?' as the two kinases drift close. Empathy fix: As the relatives are named, show a small tag 'EGFR family: EGFR, HER2, HER3' with 'active kinase' under HER2 and 'nearly inactive' under HER3.
scenes.narration: Notice that division of labor. The pressing copy only needs to supply a surface. Now pause and predict. HER2 and HER3 are relatives of the epidermal growth factor receptor. HER2 has a working kinase; HER3 barely has one. If HER2 pairs with HER3, can that mixed pair still switch on?

scenes.visual: Hold the question 'Can HER2 + HER3 still switch on?' cleanly on screen above the approaching violet HER3 and teal/amber HER2 kinases, with a subtle slow breathing motion on a gentle progress bar along the bottom edge.

scenes.tts: Yes, the mixed pair signals strongly. Nearly inactive Her three supplies the pressing large-lobe surface, switching Her two on. Whether through loop phosphorylation or lobe-to-lobe contact, the core rule holds. Bringing two receptor kinases together releases self-inhibition and activates the pair.
scenes.caption: Yes, the mixed pair signals strongly. Nearly inactive HER3 supplies the pressing large-lobe surface, switching HER2 on. Whether through loop phosphorylation or lobe-to-lobe contact, the core rule holds. Bringing two receptor kinases together releases self-inhibition and activates the pair.
scenes.visual: Dismiss the question banner. Violet HER3's large lobe presses onto amber HER2's small lobe; HER2 snaps open and glows bright active gold while HER3 stays violet. Pull back slightly to show both activation modes side by side in miniature icons below the active pair.
scenes.narration: Yes, the mixed pair signals strongly. Nearly inactive HER3 supplies the pressing large-lobe surface, switching HER2 on. Whether through loop phosphorylation or lobe-to-lobe contact, the core rule holds. Bringing two receptor kinases together releases self-inhibition and activates the pair.

scenes.tts: One lonely helix cannot twist a resting kinase awake. A ligand may bridge two chains, expose a hidden arm, or shift a pre-built pair. Either way, the payoff stays the same. Pulling two receptor kinases together opens the switch.
scenes.caption: One lonely helix cannot twist a resting kinase awake. A ligand may bridge two chains, expose a hidden arm, or shift a pre-built pair. Either way, the payoff stays the same. Pulling two receptor kinases together opens the switch.
scenes.visual: Return to the wide plasma-membrane view showing the active glowing gold receptor pair with its flexible tails beginning to shimmer below, hinting smoothly at downstream signaling without adding new labels.
scenes.narration: One lonely helix cannot twist a resting kinase awake. A ligand may bridge two chains, expose a hidden arm, or shift a pre-built pair. Either way, the payoff stays the same. Pulling two receptor kinases together opens the switch.

scenes.visual: Clean dark slate end card showing one line only, centered in large high-contrast white text: 'Bringing two receptor kinases together releases self-inhibition and activates the pair.'
